{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Central Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"5.90","formatted_progress_value2":"5.20","formatted_target_value2":"3.20","measure_header_Text2":"90th percentile physician initial assessment (PIA) time","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Halton Healthcare Services Corporation","planned_initiative":"Modify physician scheduling to ensure more consistent coverage in Zone C at the OTMH ED.","process_measure":"Our emergency department set out to reduce the time to initial physical assessment from 6.5 hours by 15% (target: 5.5 hours) through physician scheduling redesign and workflow adjustments. However, due to physician vacancies and an influx of new hires requiring orientation, we achieved an 11% improvement (5.8 hours) rather than the full target.

This initiative highlighted several key lessons. First, workforce stability is essential for sustained improvement. Without a consistent physician group, implementing new scheduling models and workflows proved challenging. Adaptability was critical, as gains were achieved through other team-led initiatives, including the implementation of standard work and lean methodologies in our cycling zones. This reinforces the importance of multi-faceted approaches, where improvements in nursing, allied health, and administrative workflows complement physician scheduling changes.

Additionally, setting realistic, incremental goals is necessary in dynamic environments. While ambitious targets drive change, staffing constraints must be factored into planning to ensure feasibility. Finally, long-term sustainability requires proactive workforce strategies, such as staggered onboarding and mentorship programs, to minimize disruptions from turnover.
Despite falling short of our target, the progress made demonstrates the value of collaboration, flexibility, and system-wide solutions in ED performance improvement. Moving forward, ensuring workforce stability while continuing to optimize ED workflows will be key to sustaining and furthering these gains.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Central Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"12.30","formatted_progress_value2":"6.90","formatted_target_value2":"8.83","measure_header_Text2":"Average Acute Length of Stay (excludes the Obstetrics Adults and Newborn patient days and discharges)","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Halton Healthcare Services Corporation","planned_initiative":"Ensure patients receive early communication of their estimated discharge date to enable timely discharge.","process_measure":"It was much more difficult to achieve the compliance targets than anticipated due to several complexities that the interprofessional team experienced when establishing an EDD. These complexities included:
• Need for Hospitalist to set EDD by day 2 in order for the primary nurse to communicate to the patient by day 3. It can be challenging to set an EDD by day 2, when patients may still not have a clear diagnosis or treatment plan.
• Physician Directed Rounds are held Monday to Friday and not on the weekend. In monitoring the data, it was noted that there was a substantial drop in EDD compliance on Mondays. It was noted that EDD compliance was best on Wednesdays and Thursdays. Future work will address the variation that occurs on the weekend.
• Setting EDDs is complex and many times the EDD is not accurate and needs to be updated based on the patient’s condition, treatments and other factors. The lack of accuracy is a source of frustration for the team as there is rework where documentation has to be updated continuously. Future work will focus on EDD accuracy.

Successes and Sustainability
As a result of the EDD project there are tools and standard work that will help spread and sustain the practice of EDD across acute care. These include:
• The Clinical Documentation Committee approved the EDD nursing intervention to become a permanent part of the Nursing Standard of Care intervention in Expanse. The Nursing Standard of Care policy will be updated to include EDD as a nursing standard of practice.
• Real time dashboards have been developed to monitor EDD compliance daily.
• An EDD tracker report can be generated from Meditech Expanse and is used by the Clinical Resource Nurse in rounds to ensure EDD is being addressed by the team.
• EDD has been approved by Clinical Documentation to be present on allied health and nursing Status Boards in Expanse. Go live date is to be determined. 
• An EDD Tri-Site working group is actively rolling out EDD in Medicine and Perioperative programs across all 3 sites. 
• EDD is/will be visible on the Hospitalist patient rosters. 
On a final note, most patients and families expressed satisfaction with having an EDD communicated to them, even if the date had to be changed. They appreciated knowing that the team is actively working on a plan and that they are engaged in that plan.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Central Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"CB","formatted_progress_value2":"100.00","formatted_target_value2":"100.00","measure_header_Text2":"Percentage of staff (identified groups) who have completed relevant EIDA-R (Equity, Inclusion, Diversity, and Anti-Racism) and FNIMUI (First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous) Cultural Safety education","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Halton Healthcare Services Corporation","planned_initiative":"Implement mandatory education for identified groups focusing on EIDA-R (Equity, Inclusion, Diversity, and Anti-Racism) and FNIMUI (First Nations, Inuit, Métis, and Urban Indigenous) Cultural Safety.","process_measure":"Our initiative set out to build upon the work done with the Executive Leadership Team in 2023/24 and expand EIDA-R and FNIMUI Cultural Safety education to our Directors, Physician Leaders and select people leaders in Human Resources and Professional Practice.  It was agreed that foundational education was necessary in order to ensure these leaders had the same baseline understanding of topics related to EIDA-R and FNIMUI before further work could be rolled out throughout the organization to support our EID-AR initiatives.  Learning from the experiences of the Executive Leadership team, we rolled out three (3) mandatory modules focusing on foundational courses addressing racial discrimination and human rights, promoting an inclusive and equitable workplace; cultural competency in healthcare; and a targeted FNIMUI course.  Overall, a post-survey assessment found that these leaders found the education to be very informative, clear and relevant providing them with the necessary context and content to understand what they did not know about these topics. 

Lessons Learned 
While informative and clear, the length of the education modules selected for this group were very long and 2 of the 3 courses could not easily be cascaded down through the organization to support our broader EIDA-R work.  Future education should consider: 
Variety in modes of education – orientation, annual core curriculum, micro-learning (think: Taking With Docs), Grand Rounds. 
Content of education - on-demand opportunities for folks to pick and choose topics that they identify needing further support with. 
With foundations established, leaders are seeking more detailed guidance about how to apply their learning and how to support the advancement of this work within our organization.  Although the initiative provided opportunities to become more informed, leaders are seeking more strategies and processes to enable providing culturally competent healthcare and inclusive spaces. 
Although pre- and post-surveys were conducted in order to gain participants’ self-evaluation of their competency before and after the training, it would have been helpful in order to consider further evaluation of the effectiveness of the training and will be incorporated as we move our EDIA-R and FNIMUI work forward here at Halton Healthcare.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Central Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"1.38","formatted_progress_value2":"1.27","formatted_target_value2":"1.17","measure_header_Text2":"Rate of workplace violence incidents that result in reportable and non-reportable injury as defined by WSIB (health care/lost time injuries/illnesses).","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Oak Valley Health","planned_initiative":"Review of personal alarm (duress tag) use.","process_measure":"Duress tag use has not been tracked before and this created challenges with record collection.  A tag use recordset was started in June 2024.
Tag use was expanded to Medicine in Winter-Spring 2024 and then Surgery, DI and Labs in fall 2024.  
Total codes have fallen from 41% to 36% since June 2024.  Over this time, both total code whites and violent events have dropped. With multiple program launches it is difficult to conclude whether one program has changed outcomes.
Tracking alone has increased focus and discussion about effectiveness of the program, which is beneficial to reviewing outcomes.  Concerns that have been reviewed from tracking include:  
o False alarms and their causes, 
o Using tags to call codes versus other devices 
Conclusion:  a 100% target is not practical nor necessarily ideal as a sign of progress for calling codes.  With the tags distributed, their effectiveness for violence prevention should continue to be reviewed and to clarify their role in preventing violence to staff.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Central Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"39.50","formatted_progress_value2":"42.20","formatted_target_value2":"31.50","measure_header_Text2":"90th percentile wait time (hours) for patients admitted from the ED to an inpatient bed or operating room, where wait time is from Disposition Date/Time until the Date/Time Patient Left Emergency Department (ED) for admission.","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Southlake Regional Health Centre","planned_initiative":"Implement an electronic Transfer of Accountability (TOA) to streamline patient handoffs while minimizing or eliminating the need for multiple phone calls. By implementing an electronic TOA system, the hospital can significantly enhance the safety and efficiency of patient transfers from the ED to inpatient units. This method focuses on creating a standardized, integrated, and user-friendly system, supported by thorough training and continuous monitoring, thereby reducing the reliance on phone calls while ensuring a high standard of patient care","process_measure":"Overall Lessons Learned: Timely bed updates and TOA completion are challenging because McKesson Performance Visibility (MPV) doesn't have automatic alerts, leading to missed updates and unexpected patient arrivals. Switching to Meditech adds complexity since its housekeeping and messaging tools are not fully developed, so staff still rely on MPV. To improve TOA consistency and address staff concerns, better training, system improvements and leadership accountability are needed, along with exploring automated messaging, dashboards and real-time feedback.","progress2":"Partially implemented as intended – full roll out April 2025 

Full Lessons Learned: 

Timely notification of bed availability and TOA completion remains a challenge due to reliance on MPV color changes without automated alerts. Inconsistent staff monitoring of MPV results in missed notifications and unexpected patient arrivals. Stronger accountability is needed to ensure bed status updates and TOA completion before transfers. 

The transition from MPV to Meditech adds complexity, requiring dual-system usage as Meditech’s housekeeping module and messaging functionality remain underdeveloped. This limits automated communication and prolongs reliance on MPV. 

Inconsistent adherence to TOA protocols has led to staff dissatisfaction, union concerns, and patient handoff issues. Addressing these concerns requires improved training, clearer expectations, and system enhancements. 

Potential Solutions & Next Steps: 

Explore activating Meditech’s messaging system for automated bed status notifications. 

Develop an ED-facing dashboard to display bed status and prompt timely TOA completion. 

Maintain verbal TOA as an optional but available clarification tool. 

Implement regular audits and real-time feedback to improve compliance. 

Investigate communication tools (Hypercare, Teams, Meditech messaging) for TOA efficiency. 

Strengthen leadership accountability measures to address non-compliance.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Toronto Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"CB","formatted_progress_value2":"26.80","formatted_target_value2":"75.00","measure_header_Text2":"Percentage of patients offered a health equity survey","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"North York General Hospital","planned_initiative":"“Everyone Counts” Health Equity Measurement Initiative: Implement a consistent approach to the collection of health equity demographic data at NYGH.","process_measure":"Accomplishments
Successful Implementation: As of November 28, 2024, the health equity survey has been fully deployed across all appropriate units at NYGH.

Enhanced Patient Outreach: Recent email collection rates averaging 35%, highlighting a significant improvement in email consent collection, enabling a more inclusive approach to digital patient engagement.

Increased Survey Response Rates: Through refined email survey invitation wording, survey response rates improved from 5.9% to 12.6% post-adjustments.

Improved Data Analytics: The Power BI dashboard allows for real-time tracking of email consent rates, response trends, and patient engagement insights.

Lessons Learned
Continuous Staff Engagement is Essential: Continuous education and engagement of frontline staff are critical to ensuring sustained compliance with email consent collection.

Technology Adaptations are Necessary: System improvements, such as automated prompts, can further reduce blank email consents.

Multi-Channel Approach Needed: While email consent is effective, additional outreach methods, such as SMS reminders or in-person follow-ups, may further improve rates.","progress2":"NYGH originally aimed to offer the survey to 75% of eligible patients but is currently trending at 50% after shifting to an email first distribution model. The organization will continue prioritizing email, targeting a 50% organization wide rate by next fiscal year while expanding in person administration in key clinical settings.
To ultimately reach 75%, NYGH must supplement email survey distribution with in-person adminstration and replicate the success of sites like Specialized Geriatric Services, where in-person administration achieves high participation and completion rates. Scaling this model will require cultural sensitivity training to engage patients effectively and meet Ontario Health mandates. This hybrid approach, combining email with direct in person engagement, ensures equitable healthcare by offering all patients, regardless of digital access or literacy, the opportunity to participate.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Toronto Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Specialty Mental Health Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"4.20","formatted_progress_value2":"3.10","formatted_target_value2":"4.80","measure_header_Text2":"% of patients physically restrained during inpatient stay","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Centre for Addiction and Mental Health","planned_initiative":"Further understand and address observed differences in the use of restraints for specific populations in the Emergency Department","process_measure":"Patient/Client Debrief Form completion: The completion rates for the Patient/Client debrief forms have shown success in establishing a process for ensuring that patients who have experienced a restraint event complete a debriefing form. The process improvements began to take hold with the involvement of Clinical Scholars, who reminded and coached staff on how to complete the debrief forms following a restraint event. However, challenges have been identified in completing the debrief forms; notably, some patients have left the emergency department (either discharged or transferred) before the forms could be completed. The insights gained from the identified challenges are guiding improvement initiatives for the 2025-26 QIP.\n\nToronto Police Services (TPS) Pilot: This pilot is an initiative to reduce restraint used in the ED, informed by research to understand and address the clinical, systemic and structural factors contributing to restraint use amongst marginalized populations.  The pilot has been successful, resulting in timely transfers of care and officers being released from the emergency department in just over an hour. {"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Toronto Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Teaching Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"15.00","formatted_progress_value2":"16.60","formatted_target_value2":"5.00","measure_header_Text2":"Choosing Wisely- Using Labs Wisely : Reduce unnecessary repeat short interval laboratory testing of lipid profiles (whole panel) for patients where testing is not indicated.","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre","planned_initiative":"Conduct Current State Analysis of SPEP/TSH/Lipid panel testing for clinical areas where repetition is not clinically indicated","process_measure":"Over the course of Q1 and Q2 we conducted a root cause analysis to identify underlying causes for frequent repeat SPEP, lipid and TSH testing. In terms of reasons for success - 
1) Utilizing Power BI Data - Based on our Power BI dashboard, we were able to readily identify provider groups who were most frequently ordering our laboratory tests of interest within the minimum retesting interval. Having this data readily availlable and stratified by clinical provider group helped us to identify key physician stakeholders who we were able to interview to gauge their insights and perspectives on the underlying root causes of repeat testing, as well as for identifying site specific criteria for appropriateness. 
2) Early and Continuous Engagement with Stakeholders - Our clinician stakeholders were experts from diverse clinical areas including Oncology, Endocrinology, Hematology, Critical Care, Nephrology, Cardiology, Stroke Neurology as well a Registered Dietician. In reflecting on our meetings with our stakeholders, we feel that key elements to successful stakeholder engagement for our team were early involvement, shared goals, as well as regular engagement and integration of stakeholder feedback into our ultimate proposal on site specific repeat testing criteria, and our intervention proposal.  
Challenges - Challenges that we identified throughout our root cause analysis and intervention design inclulded the identification of certain provider groups and clinical scenarios where more frequent repeat testing (prior to our minimum retesting criteria) are appropriate and viewed as critical to facilitating patient care. As such we did receive some pushback with regards to a universal "hard stop" intervention. An additional challenge relates to our laboratory system that would not allow us to excude certain clinicians/entire provider groups by specialty from our hard stop intervention. As such, we found we were able to most succesfully navigate these challenges by both 1) modifying our minimum retesting intervals slightly to ensure we would not be impeding the provision of patient care, and 2) create new laboratory order labels (EX: creating a new lipid panel order only for triglycerides and cholesterol that our Sunnybrook oncologists require in order to monitor patients on immunotherapy more frequently. Details around our site specific recommendations for repeat laboratory testing intervals pertaining to SPEP, TSH and lipid panels can be found in the attached word document with this submission.","progress2":"Now that we have completed our root cause analysis and refined our institution specific minimum repeat testing criteria for SPEP, lipid panels, and TSH testing (see attached) our next steps are meeting with our colleagues in the laboratory to discuss the development/implementation of our proposed hard stop interventions. The main challenges we foresee to meeting our deadline is nuances that exist with SPEP testing given this is a partially manual test (as opposed to other biochemistry tests which are automated such as lipid panels and TSH) so designing a hard stop intervention with the existing laboratory middleware system may be more complicated, but we will be meeting with the laboratory group shortly to discuss in February.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"West Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Teaching Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"61.00","formatted_progress_value2":"57.00","formatted_target_value2":"64.00","measure_header_Text2":"Patient Safety Culture Survey - ‘Overall Rating Score’?","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"London Health Sciences Centre","planned_initiative":"Implementation of Continuous Improvement of Care","process_measure":"YES: This change idea was implemented.
Continuous Improvement of Care is a method of driving quality and safety at all levels of the organization. It provides a platform to empower staff and physicians to solve problems and improve outcomes while advancing a culture of evidence-informed decisions.  
LHSC’s Quality, Patient Safety and Performance regularly offers two trainings for all staff and a training for new leaders. Training is mandatory for all leaders and optional for all other staff.  The Structured Problem Solving course focuses on how teams can use continuous improvement of care tools to improve their processes. The session focuses on how to use a structured method to identify, discuss and solve problems that occur. The Supporting Collaborative Improvement session focuses on how to work on collaborative improvements and what to do with larger problems that come up within the team. 
Status exchanges and huddles occur across the organization with a designated quality and patient safety consultant for each of the clinical areas. 
Lesson Learned
Due to organizational changes this year, the implementation of the executive management system was revised several times. This was to ensure alignment with new organizational priorities. Sustainability of Continuous Improvement of Care requires that the organization embed the tools into quality and performance structures.  The development of LHSC’s Integrated Quality Management Plan will focus on how the organization has a systematic and structured approach for maintaining and providing high quality care.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"West Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Teaching Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"61.00","formatted_progress_value2":"57.00","formatted_target_value2":"64.00","measure_header_Text2":"Patient Safety Culture Survey - ‘Overall Rating Score’?","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"London Health Sciences Centre","planned_initiative":"Improved Serious Safety Event Process","process_measure":"YES: This change idea was implemented.
This year there has been an increased emphasis on the importance of closing the loop with staff members following patient safety incidents. To improve the consistency with which leaders are providing support and closure to staff following incidents and incident reporting, increased emphasis has been placed on completing follow-up or closing the loop with staff. The improvements that have been completed over the past year include a formal reporting process for leaders through the quality of care review presentation for all serious safety events.  Leaders are engaging with staff who submitted adverse event reports, and those involved in a serious safety event to provide support, and include these staff in the review process. In addition, expectations have been established for leaders to communicate the recommendations from serious safety events to those directly impacted/involved, to their department, as well as more broadly across the organization or like programs as applicable.
In addition to the closing the loop processes within the serious safety event process, a process has also been created through the SPEAK event management system to improve communication with staff following any adverse event, near miss, or good catch. Through the SPEAK system, leaders can directly enter their follow-up process and gratitude to the staff for entering the event. In addition, staff can access the events they have entered to monitor progress and updates from leaders. LHSC is finalizing the LHSC Disclosure Policy, that has included engagement with leadership and patient partners and helps to solidify expectations and accountabilities for closing the loop.   
From a patient perspective, the expectation for disclosure that a review is occurring following a serious safety event has been established with leaders. With the support of patient relations, these conversations are occurring more frequently allowing the opportunity for transparency, and closure for patients and families impacted by a serious safety event.  In addition, this process allows patients and families the opportunity to share their perspectives and ask questions that they would like included within the review process. To support this ongoing disclosure, the Disclosure of Patient Harm procedure has been revised and is currently in the process of review and finalization.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

This year, 86 physicians have enrolled to work on initiatives focused on either completing discharge summaries within 48 hours or improving discharge medication reconciliation processes. {"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Toronto Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"","formatted_current_value2":"7.80","formatted_progress_value2":"4.20","formatted_target_value2":"7.00","measure_header_Text2":"Percentage of reported workplace violence incidents that resulted in health care and lost time","methods":"N","org_name_Text2":"Unity Health Toronto","planned_initiative":"Leverage EPIC to understand ABC policy compliance and implement strategies to increase compliance with the Violence Assessment tool (VAT) and Safety Plan.","process_measure":"Successes: 
• Consistently achieved 80-90% compliance with the Violence Assessment Tool (VAT) in the Emergency Department (ED).
• Utilized EPIC reporting functionalities to monitor compliance metrics in real-time, enabling timely interventions and targeted education efforts.
• Increased staff awareness and engagement through ongoing education and feedback, contributing to higher compliance rates.
• Developed reports within EPIC that facilitated tracking progress and identifying patterns of non-compliance.

Challenges: 
• Safety plan compliance remained inconsistent, with some units or providers demonstrating lower adherence despite awareness efforts.
• Variability in documentation practices and understanding of safety plan requirements led to gaps in compliance.
• Time constraints and high patient volumes in the ED sometimes hindered thorough completion of safety plans.

Barriers: 
• Need for additional training on safety plan components, which contributes to inconsistent completion. 
• Workflow disruptions and competing priorities during busy shifts affected compliance.
• Variability in staff engagement levels with safety plan protocols.

Enablers: 
• Strong leadership support emphasizing the importance of safety and compliance.
• Availability of EPIC reports that provided transparent, accessible compliance data for staff and leadership.
• Ongoing targeted education sessions and reminders embedded within EPIC workflows.
• Interdisciplinary collaboration to refine documentation processes and address barriers.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"Central Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"22.69","formatted_progress_value2":"28.04","formatted_target_value2":"21.56","measure_header_Text2":"Daily average number of patients waiting in the emergency department for an inpatient bed at 8 a.m.","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Halton Healthcare Services Corporation","planned_initiative":"Create a new pathway for Halton@Home from the Emergency Department to avoid admission.","process_measure":"Several key lessons emerged through implementation. Sustained growth in ED diversion and admission avoidance is highly dependent on stable outpatient clinic capacity and program scale of the ED Admission Avoidance Pathway. While the development of a comprehensive ambulatory clinic catalogue was foundational, it proved more complex than anticipated due to vendor constraints and operational variability across programs; as a result, the organization prioritized high-volume, high-impact clinics to support early gains while broader capability is developed. In parallel, limitations in existing data and workflows restricted the reliable identification of patients whose admission is driven primarily by discharge planning or social care needs, limiting the ability to proactively apply alternative care pathways. Experience also demonstrated that education and awareness, while necessary, are insufficient in isolation to produce consistent decision-making. Greater impact is achieved through system-level enablers embedded directly into clinical workflows, including automated identification of patients already connected to home and community-based services. These learnings reinforced the importance of moving toward higher-reliability interventions, such as workflow notifications and integrated decision support, to enable admission avoidance. 

Building on FY25/26 progress, FY26/27 efforts will focus on system-level flow improvements, including strengthened inter-facility transfers, standardized ALC management, and expanded short-stay and virtual care models to further reduce early-morning ED congestion.","progress2":"+NB: Ontario Health introduced NBA last year as a QIP indicator, and used previous performance data based on Q1 and Q2 in 2024 only. Current performance is based on the full fiscal year of 2024/25, which does not align with the QIP workplan for 2025/26, which started on April 1, 2025. This makes it an unreasonable measure of current performance based on QIP improvements. Since April 1, 2025, January YTD performance on NBA is 23.31, which shows a YTD improvement of 17% versus a reported 23.58% worsening of performance.  

To improve patient flow and reduce avoidable admissions, two key initiatives were implemented: a formal ED to Halton@Home admission avoidance pathway and expanded ED referrals to priority ambulatory clinics, which increased by 13.5% year over year. These pathways were embedded into ED workflows through clearer eligibility criteria and targeted case finding. Patient outcomes remained strong, with a 30-day readmission rate of approximately 5%, well below the <10% target, confirming safe and appropriate diversion to outpatient care. 

Of note, one process measure was incorrectly entered as a target of 20 referrals per week; the intended target was 20 referrals per month, with planned scaling as program capacity developed. As the program scaled, we made steady progress towards the target and were able to exceed our targets by the first month of Q4.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

Implementation focused on strengthening reliable clinical practice and data integrity. Documentation gaps—particularly capture of Braden scores below 18 and confirmation of prevention interventions—were addressed through routine quarterly audits in high-risk areas, supporting validation of hospital-acquired pressure injury incidents and improving confidence in performance data. 

To enable sustained harm reduction, the organization prioritized standardized, equitable access to pressure-relieving equipment, initiating replacement of non–pressure-relieving surfaces with pressure-reducing surfaces, starting in highest-prevalence areas.

Outcome data demonstrated sustained and meaningful improvement. • A hot wash debrief occurs immediately following an incident, and
• A cold wash debrief follows to further explore learning opportunities.

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"50","formatted_progress_value2":"53","formatted_target_value2":"30","measure_header_Text2":"90th percentile ambulance offload time","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Pembroke Regional Hospital Inc.","planned_initiative":"Reduce the time it takes to offload patients from ambulances to the Emergency Department by enhancing communication, optimizing the handover process, and improving coordination between ambulance teams and Emergency Department staff.","process_measure":"This year's Ambulance Offload Time (AOT) QIP reinforced the importance of adaptability. As the QIP progressed, several planned interventions required additional refinement. For example, our updated paramedic arrival notification process saw multiple iterations, ultimately taking more time than was anticipated. Detailed reviews also identified the need for more accurate and consistent data capture to reflect true AOT performance, highlighting further opportunities for improvement. External factors influenced progress as well, such as the temporary unavailability of the on-site primary care paramedic during a critical period (October to January).  Overall, these experiences emphasized that while we may begin with a specific plan, change idea, or countermeasure, we also must be willing to adapt. When an approach is not producing desired results, it is essential to explore and test alternatives co-designed with those doing the work and using a structured problem-solving approach.","progress2":"Please note that, as of February 2026, PRH's 90th percentile AOT performance has improved to 39min. See attached for a month-by-month breakdown of AOT performance for FY 25/26.\n\nThis QIP driver has positioned PRH for continued improvement in offload time performance. Key accomplishments include the development of a county-wide Fit2Sit program; offload huddle implementation; arrival notification process enhancements; and our new \"direct to CT\" pathway for eligible patients. Fit2Sit, initially a PRH-specific initiative developed in collaboration with our paramedic partners, has since expanded across the county and has shown early signs of positive patient response and improved paramedic turnaround. The addition of \"offload huddles\", bringing together EMS, the PRH Triage RN, and the Primary Care Paramedic, has reduced duplication in handover, strengthened communication, and further optimized transfer of care in the ED. Additionally, gains were achieved through enhancements to our ambulance arrival-notification processes and implementation of our \"direct-to-CT\" pathway for eligible interfacility arrivals to support faster diagnostics and improved patient flow.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"CB","formatted_progress_value2":"NA","formatted_target_value2":"70.00","measure_header_Text2":"Percentage of patients at risk for delirium who have at least one prevention strategy documented in their care plan.","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Pembroke Regional Hospital Inc.","planned_initiative":"Enhance delirium early detection, intervention strategies, and management of delirium to reduce its impact during hospitalization, reducing the severity of delirium and promoting better patient outcomes and safety.","process_measure":"Please note: PRH's delirium QIP driver changed significantly over the course of 25/26. Our revised methods and process measures for this were as follows:

Methods: Establish a collaborative team consisting of healthcare professionals from various disciplines to review and assess current delirium management strategies. Formalize a method to educate frontline staff and evaluate patient screening for delirium. Establish a process for evaluating process measure(s). Leverage the expertise of the working group to identify areas for improvement and implement evidence-based practices that optimize delirium intervention. Additionally, work to enhance protocols for early identification and timely management of delirium.

Process measures:
- Percentage of frontline staff who have received education on delirium risk factors, screening tools, and prevention methods. Target: 70%

- Percentage of patients with CAM positive screening who have at least one intervention strategy documented. Q3 Target: 60%

- Percentage of patients with CAM positive screening who have at least one intervention strategy documented. Q4 Target: 70%

Over the course of this year, our Delirium Prevention QIP revealed an important gap between established delirium screening practices and variability in managing delirium for patients who screen positive. This recognition prompted a key shift in our objective from identifying delirium risk to strengthening delirium management. Education to staff was foundational for this driver. Focusing on delivering content in a manner that was consistent, paced, and predictable helped to prevent overwhelming staff. Additional "just-in-time" coaching complemented education to enhance learnings and the application of knowledge. Anecdotally, we have also observed more purposeful use of the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) tool across our hospital in assessing for delirium.","progress2":"As PRH prepares for significant workflow changes with the upcoming 2026 Epic implementation, this year's work has helped consolidate improvements in delirium management that we aim to preserve through this transition. Our focus is on ensuring gains are carried forward and integrated into new processes post Epic Go-Live.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

This will reduce frustration and enhance overall patient and family satisfaction.","process_measure":"Over the course of the year, several key lessons emerged from our Patient Experience in the Emergency Department (ED) driver. While our frontline-developed Q&A resource to improve messaging consistency was well-received pre-implementation, formal evaluation post-implementation highlighted a need for deeper understanding and a potential redesign to optimize value. We also learned our evaluation timelines were insufficient. Delays and limited dedicated time for formal evaluation left too little time to thoroughly evaluate effectiveness of some interventions. Additionally, stronger-than-anticipated baseline patient experience data reduced room for measurable quantitative improvement, prompting a shift toward qualitative data analysis to identify opportunities for improvement while aiming to maintain quantitative patient survey performance.","progress2":"Despite challenges, this QIP project highlighted the critical importance of engaging all areas of the ED in shaping, refining, and implementing improvement efforts. Patient feedback guided us beyond communication-focused initiatives, prompting practical enhancements such as better climate control and access to cellphone chargers in the department. Although the initial target was to implement two improvements, ongoing feedback revealed additional opportunities. Ultimately, we implemented eight improvement ideas including improved signage, registration tablet usability improvements, and refinements to staff assignments in the ED to better support the overall patient experience.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Large Community Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"66.00","formatted_progress_value2":"70.00","formatted_target_value2":"75.00","measure_header_Text2":"Percentage of respondents who select “Always” or “Completely” to the following questions:  “Were your family or friends involved as much as you wanted in decisions about your care and treatment?” “When you left the hospital, did you have a better understanding of your condition than when you entered?”","methods":"N","org_name_Text2":"Pembroke Regional Hospital Inc.","planned_initiative":"To assess and improve communication about discharge with inpatients, focusing on enhancing patient knowledge of their condition and satisfaction with family/caregiver involvement.","process_measure":"A number of key lessons learned emerged from this year's Discharge Communication QIP, including:

1. Value of the Teach Back Method: Consistent use of the Teach Back method has been identified as an important skill in enhancing patient and family/caregiver discharge communication. The Teach Back method helps staff understand how to communicate information meaningfully by having patients/caregivers repeat education back, in their own words. This also provides in-the-moment feedback to staff on opportunities to revise their approach and strengthen subsequent teaching. Patient and staff feedback indicate that broader use of this method can improve comprehension and confidence.

2. Consistent Use of Patient Whiteboards: Patient and caregiver feedback emphasized how important patient whiteboards are as a communication tool. For example, our whiteboards can help to identify who a patient wants involved in their care; enhance communication between patient/family/caregivers and care team; and provide valuable and accessible key updates at-a-glance. Continued focus is needed to support reliable, organization-wide adoption of whiteboard practices to ensure patients receive these important updates more consistently.

3. Identifying and leveraging Family/Caregiver "Key Moments": Work with frontline teams identified many "Key Moments" when engaging family/caregivers may have the greatest impact. These insights helped determine department-specific and organization-wide opportunities for enhancing family/caregiver involvement; however, momentum on this decreased over the course of the year to focus on other priorities for this QIP driver. Sustained and renewed attention may help to maximize the benefits of these insights.

4. Balancing Competing Priorities During Quality Improvement Work: Teams initially planned regular QIP-related discussions during departmental quality improvement huddles, though operational demands at times reduced the frequency and depth of these conversations over the course of the year. This affected frontline engagement and overall progress on implementation of change ideas. Finding more sustainable balance, combined with exploring additional opportunities for frontline engagement, may improve consistency and performance moving forward.","progress2":"While our performance on this indicator did improve compared to baseline, we did not meet our target and recognize the need for continued focus in this area. Meaningful progress was made in advancing several foundational initiatives; however, challenges with consistent application across units became apparent. Throughout the year we gained clarity on impactful strategies, such as standardizing use of teach back method and ensuring reliable use of patient whiteboards. These efforts have laid important groundwork; though looking ahead to the 2026/27 QIP cycle, also indicate a need to continue to adapt our approach in implementing these strategies fully across our hospital.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

Organize a Kaizen event to identify actionable items to improve PIA.","process_measure":"We have demonstrated improvement in Emergency Department (ED) metrics over the past year; however, there remains room for further improvement. All change ideas identified in the 2025/26 Quality Improvement (QI) Plan have been implemented. Over this period, we have experienced a significant increase in ED patient volume, particularly among high-acuity patients. HRH has also seen a substantial rise in EMS transfers and continues to receive a higher number of ambulances compared to other GTA hospitals, with more CTAS 1–2 patients being transferred. Even with this increased demand, we have achieved measurable improvements in ED performance. We will continue to work collaboratively with the ED and HRH teams to achieve target performance, with a focused emphasis on PIA, EMS offload times, and inpatient bed turnaround time. Notably, for the third consecutive year, we are ranked the #1 Emergency Department in the province based on P4R performance.

Impact of the Change Ideas:
The change ideas had a clear positive impact, helping streamline workflows, improve patient flow, and maintain performance despite rising demand. For example, targeted interventions in PIA and EMS offload contributed to reducing delays and supporting better overall ED efficiency.

Over the past year, we experienced a significant increase in ED patient volume, particularly among high-acuity patients (CTAS 1–2), as well as an increase in EMS transfers compared to other GTA hospitals. Despite these pressures, we successfully implemented all change ideas outlined in the 2025/26 QI Plan and were able to demonstrate measurable improvement in key ED metrics, including PIA, EMS offload times, and inpatient bed turnaround time.","progress2":"Key Learnings:
1. Collaboration across the ED, HRH, and operational teams is critical to sustaining improvements, especially during periods of high patient volume.
2. Early identification of bottlenecks, such as EMS offload and inpatient bed flow, allows targeted interventions that can have significant impact.
3. Leadership is essential to achieving improvement; guiding teams, fostering engagement, and supporting change makes a measurable difference.
4. When implementing change ideas, it is important to remain open-minded and continuously monitor results. Improvement in one metric may necessitate workflow adjustments elsewhere to ensure balanced performance across the system.
5. Even when patient acuity and volume increase, structured QI initiatives can still drive meaningful improvements if change ideas are fully implemented and monitored.

Advice to Others:
• Fully implement and monitor all change ideas; partial implementation limits impact.
• Engage front-line staff early and maintain ongoing communication to ensure buy-in and sustainability.
• Track key metrics regularly to identify trends, celebrate improvements, and quickly address emerging challenges.
• Recognize that even during periods of high acuity and volume, structured QI approaches can yield measurable gains.
• Strong leadership is key—leaders must guide, motivate, and support teams to achieve meaningful improvement.
• Be open-minded and continuously reassess workflows; improvements in one area may require adjustments elsewhere to maintain overall system efficiency.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

Through a QI initiative on two acute inpatient units, there was a sustained increase in CAM tool completion from 4% and 2% to 52% and 74%, respectively.

100% of adult inpatient units were provided with education sessions and huddles focused talks related to Delirium.

Through a point-in-time audit in one emergency department, 73% of applicable patients and families indicated awareness of delirium prevention strategies while in the ED.

Successes, Challenges, Barriers, and Enablers:
A key enabler of our work is our highly engaged team and the fact that delirium is on our Care for Older Persons Strategy, which is an organizational priority. A success of our work has been increased awareness of delirium amongst staff, patients, and families. One way we did this was by rounding at all sites with our Patient Partner to share her lived experience of delirium. Another success is the QI work we did to increase CAM tool completion on two acute inpatient units through an education intervention. Barriers and challenges impacting our work include competing priorities in the organization and the need to optimize our new HIS to meet our needs.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Small Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"34","formatted_progress_value2":"40","formatted_target_value2":"30","measure_header_Text2":"90th percentile ambulance offload time","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Arnprior Regional Health","planned_initiative":"Implementation of more efficient processes and better coordination with EMS.","process_measure":"ARH made progress this year on improving the accuracy and consistency of ambulance offload time data, though the overall target was not met due to data‑quality issues.

Successes
-Improved data integrity: Significant reconciliation work in Q2–Q3 strengthened alignment between ED operations and health records  

-Growing staff awareness: Daily coaching, improved understanding of offload time documentation requirements.

-Foundational structures built: Biweekly and weekly audit processes were developed, providing the basis for more reliable monitoring.

Challenges
-Data-quality inconsistencies between operations and ED systems required extensive manual correction, delaying progress. Absence of business intelligence tool requires significant manual data manipulation. 

-Operational pressures and a shift in leadership impacted the team’s ability to complete audits regularly early in the year.

-Delayed audit implementation due to the need to focus on historical data cleanup.

Results, Barriers, and Enablers

Results: Documentation completeness and time‑stamping accuracy improved steadily through late Q3 and into Q4 as data quality stabilized.

Barriers: System discrepancies, high workloads, delayed audits, and variable familiarity with documentation standards with a high turnover of staff.

Enablers: Strong ED–Health Records  collaboration, consistent coaching, engaged frontline staff, and standardized audit tools.

Summary
Although ARH did not meet the offload time target this fiscal year, substantial groundwork was completed. With improved data quality and strengthened documentation processes, ARH enters the next fiscal year with a more reliable foundation for monitoring and improving ambulance offload performance. In addition, members of the front-line team feel as though the current data is consistently reporting a higher AOL than what what is occurring operationally.","progress2":"There is an ongoing collaboration with the ED staff and Health Records to ensure that data reporting is accurate and reflects day-to-day ED operations. Many of the data points being utilized in FY 25/26 were inaccurate and did not reflect the patient journey from Ambulance arrival to Offload.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Small Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"4.67","formatted_progress_value2":"4.90","formatted_target_value2":"4.00","measure_header_Text2":"90th percentile emergency department wait time to physician initial assessment","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Arnprior Regional Health","planned_initiative":"Capture accurate PIA especially related to high acuity cases.","process_measure":"ARH continued its work this fiscal year to improve the accuracy and reliability of PIA data for CTAS 1 and 2 patients, with a focus on reviewing high‑acuity cases and identifying EMR workflows that better capture physician initial assessment times. Although progress was made in establishing review processes and standardizing workflows, ARH did not meet the target, with current performance at 4.9 hours compared to the provincial target of 4.0 and 4.67 last year.

Successes

- Regular review of high‑acuity cases: ARH increased oversight of CTAS 1 and 2 charts, particularly where PIA exceeded one hour. These reviews created a clearer understanding of workflow delays and documentation gaps.

- Improved collaboration with ED physicians: Engaging physicians in discussions about PIA performance helped identify peak volume times and potential opportunities to improve coverage and flow.

-EMR workflow exploration: Preliminary work was completed to map current documentation practices and assess where additional Meditech workflows could support more accurate capture of PIA times. In addition conversations have begun related to how PIA will be captured in future state EPIC (Oct 2026) 

Challenges

- Worsening PIA performance: Higher patient acuity and increased ED volumes compared to our regional peers and compared to previous years contributed to longer PIA times and added pressure on physician resources.

- Data accuracy issues: Similar to ambulance offload reporting, PIA data often did not reflect real clinical activity. Physicians frequently did not use the Meditech functions designed to record PIA, leading to under‑captured or inaccurate timestamps.

- Incomplete adoption of EMR workflows: Identifying additional EMR solutions proved difficult within the current system capabilities in addition to navigating resistance to change within the ED MD group. 

Process Measures: Results, Barriers, and Enablers

Results: Reviews of high‑acuity cases improved understanding of workflow challenges, though the goal of reviewing 100% of CTAS 1 and 2 cases with PIA > 1 hour by Q4 was not consistently met due to competing operational priorities. EMR workflow improvements were assessed but not fully implemented.

Barriers: Rising acuity and volume, inconsistent physician use of Meditech PIA functions, limitations within the current EMR, and operational pressures impacting timely documentation. Lack of a Business Intelligence tool at ARH means that all extraction and validation are done manually, requiring significant staff time and slowing improvement efforts

Enablers: Engagement of ED physicians in data review, strengthened collaboration across the P4R working group in particular Health Records, growing awareness of documentation expectations, and improved analytics capacity to support case review.","progress2":"Although PIA performance did not meet targets this year, ARH strengthened its understanding of documentation challenges, gained clearer insight into physician coverage needs, and laid groundwork for EMR and workflow improvements leading into the implementation of EPIC. These steps position the organization for more targeted progress in the next fiscal year.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Small Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"0.14","formatted_progress_value2":"0.15","formatted_target_value2":"0.14","measure_header_Text2":"Daily average number of patients waiting in the emergency department for an inpatient bed at 8 a.m.","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"Arnprior Regional Health","planned_initiative":"Look for opportunities to streamline the admission process and improving bed management practices.","process_measure":"ARH continues to monitor the number of admitted patients remaining in ED spaces at 0800. Performance this year is 0.15, slightly above last year’s 0.14, this has been reported as a 7.14% decline. Based on operational review, this change is likely related to patients with high acuity or complexity being admitted but remaining in the ED until clinically stable enough for the inpatient unit (IPU). This practice has contributed to higher counts of admitted patients occupying ED spaces at the morning reporting time.

Successes
- Improved understanding of patient flow issues: Case reviews helped clarify that increases in the 0800 metric relate more to patient acuity and appropriateness for the IPU than to bed availability alone.

- Progress toward policy standardization: Work is well underway on a policy to guide physicians in determining which patients are appropriate for admission to the IPU versus those who must remain in the ED until stable. This includes safe handover practices and clarity around MRP at specific times of day. 

- Strengthened cross‑department collaboration: Multiple committees and clinical stakeholders have contributed to policy development, improving alignment across the organization.

Challenges
- Premature admissions to IPU: Some patients who are not yet clinically appropriate for the IPU are being admitted, increasing the count of admitted patients remaining in ED spaces at 0800. 

- High-acuity patient volumes: Higher acuity levels in the ED mean more patients require extended stabilization in the ED before transfer to an inpatient bed.

- Ongoing practice variability: Despite progress, there is still inconsistency in how physicians determine readiness for transfer to the IPU.

Results, Barriers, and Enablers
Results: The number of admitted patients in ED spaces at 0800 increased minimally from 0.14 to 0.15. While not a significant operational change, it exceeds the target of maintaining or improving performance.

Barriers: Lack of a standardized policy guiding physician decision‑making for IPU appropriateness.
High acuity setting placing pressure on ED space and workflow.

Enablers: Active policy development with broad stakeholder engagement. Increased awareness among physicians and leaders regarding the impact of early admission decisions. Improved communication between ED and inpatient teams.","progress2":"Although ARH reported a slight decline in performance for admitted patients in ED spaces at 0800, this trend is closely linked to patient acuity and challenges determining IPU readiness rather than a deterioration of patient flow. With a new policy nearing completion, increased cross‑team collaboration, and growing awareness of appropriate admission criteria, ARH is positioned to stabilize and improve performance in the coming fiscal year.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

Priority action will be to maintain funding. Implementing innovative digital solutions will alleviate over-crowding and increase safety.","process_measure":"Triage Reassessment Nurse Role 
  The implementation of the Triage Reassessment Nurse role has contributed to a reduction in patients leaving without being seen (LWBS) by ensuring regular reassessment, timely escalation of care, and improved monitoring of patients waiting for physician assessment. 

Virtual Home Waiting Room 
  The ED Virtual Home Waiting Room has demonstrated positive impact with reductions in time to Physician Initial Assessment (PIA), LWBS rates, and overall Emergency Department length of stay. In addition, patient feedback indicates improved satisfaction related to reduced waiting room congestion and the ability to wait at home. 

Flow Nurse Role, Chair Care Model, and Additional Waiting Areas 
  The combination of the Flow Nurse role, expanded hallway recliner chair capacity, and additional internal waiting spaces has improved patient flow throughout the department. These initiatives have supported more efficient use of treatment rooms and contributed to reductions in overall length of stay (LOS). 

Staff Engagement and Adoption of New Initiatives 
  Successful engagement of nursing and physician staff has supported the implementation of multiple new roles and processes. Front‑line involvement and acceptance of these changes have been key to embedding improvements into daily operations and sustaining progress toward improved PIA performance. 

Challenges 

Inpatient Overcapacity Impacting ED Flow 
  Ongoing overcapacity in inpatient units has limited the availability of inpatient beds, contributing to congestion within the Emergency Department and delays in patient movement. This has had downstream impacts on treatment room availability and time to Physician Initial Assessment (PIA). To mitigate this, a new organizational surge plan has been implemented to support earlier escalation and improved coordination across programs. As this surge plan is relatively new, there continue to be implementation and workflow adjustment challenges as teams adapt to new processes. 

Physician Coverage and Staffing Constraints 
  Consistent physician coverage remains a challenge due to a provincial reduction of physician hours by approximately 11 hours per day, compounded by ongoing physician recruitment challenges. Reduced physician availability can impact the sustainability of early‑assessment improvements and timely PIA performance, particularly during peak volumes and surge periods. 

Mitigation Strategies for Medical Staffing Challenges 
  To help offset physician staffing constraints, the ED has implemented mitigation strategies including the utilization of Nurse Practitioners (NPs) and Physician Assistants (PAs), in addition to ongoing process improvements. While these strategies have supported care delivery and patient flow, physician coverage remains a key risk to sustaining PIA performance improvements.","progress2":"mplement a Physician “Casino Shifts” from 10pm – 4am and 4am – 10am to help clear the backup patients in the late evening and assist with early discharges.

Establish a corporate plan to enable ongoing hospital- wide excellence in providing Language Concordant Care once the implementation support of this QIP comes to an end.","process_measure":"In order to be successful, sustainability planning requires partnerships across multiple departments. The essential elements for ongoing improvement were identified, and collaborations were established with the departments and teams who have aligned operation oversight:

a. Language Concordant Care added to corporate orientation (day one, all staff) in partnership with Interprofessional Practice as part of the Person Centred Care Module, as access to first language care aligns closely with the 3 vital behaviours.

b. Maintenance of the staff-facing hub will be a collaboration between the Interpreter Services department and Strategic Communications.

c. Accessing interpreters usually relies on hardware (phones/tablets/WOWs). QIP team met with Client Services to share the most common technology-based failures to accessing an interpreter we encountered while completing change idea 1. Based on those lessons-learned, Client Services made adjustments to the weekly hardware rounds performed on inpatient units (added 2 tasks to support early detection of hardware failure)

Sustainability Plans not part of initial QIP submission

1. Incorporate LCC into training for learners, complete for 81% of learner categories at Sunnybrook.
2. Transition dashboard reporting Language Concordant Care from quality priority to permanent operations
3. Quarterly review of interpreter service use by LCC team and Client Service in 2026/27. Group will monitor usage rates and address any continued areas of challenge and/or drops in usage","progress2":"n/a","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

Targeted role optimization supports improvement: Efforts to optimize advanced practice provider roles and physician scheduling contributed to measurable improvement in PIA performance, even where targets were not fully met. 

Data visibility supported decision‑making: Use of ED performance dashboards (including hourly PIA views) enabled better understanding of demand patterns and supported more informed operational discussions.

Challenges 

PIA remains constrained by downstream flow: Improvements in PIA were limited by broader ED congestion, including inpatient bed availability and high volumes of admitted patients boarding in the ED, reinforcing that PIA cannot be solved in isolation. 

Mismatch between peak demand and resourcing: Performance challenges were more pronounced during peak arrival periods (e.g., late afternoon/evening EMS surges), highlighting the need for tighter alignment between staffing models and true demand patterns. 

System‑level dependencies persist: Similar to ambulance offload, PIA performance is vulnerable to external and upstream pressures (seasonality, surgical slowdowns, discharge delays), requiring coordinated, cross‑portfolio action.","progress2":"tbd","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

This year the ED completed the self‑assessment and development of action plans for both LHSC’s University Hospital and Victoria Hospital in response to Ontario Health’s Emergency Department Leading Practices Toolkit. Developing these action plans ensured that both hospitals have a clear roadmap for implementing evidence‑informed strategies that support flow, safety, and patient experience.
Both locations completed value stream mapping activities based on the Leading Practices Toolkit. These exercises provided a detailed assessment of the patient journey within each ED, identifying inefficiencies and prioritizing targeted improvements. The value stream maps offer a critical foundation for future PDSA cycles, as they make flow barriers more visible and support data‑driven decision‑making. 
Together, this work demonstrates meaningful progress toward improving system flow through structured improvement methods and enhanced alignment with provincial guidance. Continued focus on testing and refining interventions will be essential for ensuring patients move efficiently through the system.","progress2":"","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital"}

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"West Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Teaching Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"5.90","formatted_progress_value2":"5.80","formatted_target_value2":"6.00","measure_header_Text2":"90th percentile emergency department wait time to physician initial assessment","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"London Health Sciences Centre","planned_initiative":"Physician Schedule Improvement Strategy","process_measure":"The ED focused on filling physician scheduling gaps by adding targeted shifts to improve ED flow. A key accomplishment was the implementation and ongoing PDSA testing of the Pod D INT 2.0 zone at Victoria Hospital, supported by a dedicated physician from 2 to 10 p.m. to reduce Left Without Being Seen (LWBS) rates and Physician Initial Assessment (PIA) times.
Interdisciplinary collaboration also played a major role in improving flow. At University Hospital, health disciplines expanded their coverage to support timely assessments and safe discharge home, helping reduce unnecessary admissions. At Victoria Hospital, the introduction of a Nurse Practitioner in October 2025 added independent clinical capacity and provided a consistent resource for patients and staff. This year updates were made to the Medical Advisory Committee (MAC) ED Admission Guidelines, accompanied by enhanced reporting processes to support practice change. These updates provided clearer expectations for admission standards and improved accountability.

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"West Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Teaching Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"CB","formatted_progress_value2":"50.00","formatted_target_value2":"CB","measure_header_Text2":"Average Emergency Department Wait Time to Physician Initial Assessment for Individuals with Sickle Cell Disease (CTAS 1 or 2)","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"London Health Sciences Centre","planned_initiative":"Complete a deep dive into the reliability of data to ensure appropriateness in setting meaningful improvement targets.","process_measure":"YES:  This change idea was implemented.

Throughout the year, the reporting processes were refined to ensure accuracy, especially given that the baseline year establishes the foundation for target setting. Through this work, it was determined that a one quarter data lag was necessary to ensure all patient encounters were correctly coded and complete, providing reliable volume counts and accurate wait‑time data. {"LHIN_Label_Text2":"West Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Teaching Hospital","formatted_current_value2":"70.00","formatted_progress_value2":"71.00","formatted_target_value2":"73.50","measure_header_Text2":"To improve in-patient experience survey results related to information at discharge by 5%","methods":"Y","org_name_Text2":"St. Joseph's Health Care System Hamilton","planned_initiative":"Implementation of strategies to address patient experience","process_measure":"Throughout the year the QIP working group undertook and explored and implemented many change ideas, including the following:
1. Patient Partnership Lead completed phone survey and paper survey of recent discharges to gain input on information provided at discharge and any opportunities for improvement over approximately 2-week period. Results were very positive and provided minimal insights to create additional change ideas. 
2. Introduction of volunteer program to meet with new admissions twice weekly, to explain the Patient Experience Survey, gain consent for electronic distribution and collection of email address. 
3. Explored additional information provision as part of After Visit Summary (AVS). 
4. Exploration of adjusting the expressed consent requirement to implied consent to reduce barriers to survey distribution; environmental scan completed; direction from legal/risk to proceed with moving to implied consent with hopes to increase response rates; work to commence in May once Dovetale upgrade implemented. 
5. Introduction of QR codes to After Visit Summaries to increase survey completion on December 2, 2025. QR codes bypass need for expressed consent. 

Additionally, new information relevant to the adoption of the survey and challenges were realized throughout the year, including:
1. Completing a deep dive on the question asked on the survey. Question is not as simple as “did you receive enough information at discharge” full question is Did you receive enough information from hospital staff about what to do if you were worried about your condition or treatment after you left the hospital?; concerns were raised around framing of question impacting the response. Consultation with Ontario Hospital Association occurred to understand development process of question (and larger survey); inability to reframe question if we wish to continue to peer benchmark. 
2. Peer Benchmarking became available in Q2; Peer benchmarking is still considered exploratory and provisional; peer benchmarking focused on Top 2 box (response of completely and usually) not Top Box which was unknown when establishing QIP.  
 Based on Top 2 Box, the two clinical units perform well on Information at discharge question averaging 89% on 6GI and 91% for 3OBs between April 2025- February 2026. This information would have adjusted the proposed QIP from top box to top 2 boxes.
3. Additionally, due to some updates within Qualtrics and working through unforeseen impacts to SJHH, SJHH survey distribution was paused between September 29 and December 12, 2025. Survey has resumed, and a bolus of survey distribution occurred on December 14, 2025, for patients who met criteria during the pause to distribution.

{"LHIN_Label_Text2":"North East Region","OrgCategory_Label_Text2":"Small Hospital","aim_header_Text2":"Timely","comments2":"Improvement initiatives for both Ambulance Offload Time (AOT) and Physician Initial Assessment (PIA) focus on optimizing front-end patient flow within the Emergency Department. Schedule primary care provider and team to attend the building.","sector_name_Text2":"Acute Care/Hospital","target_justification2":"Introduction
The Neighbourhood Care Team (NCT) is a Primary Care Geriatric Integrated Team that unites health care organizations, 
providers, and their clients (patients, families, and caregivers), to improve the integration and coordination of care and 
operate as ‘one team’ in the eyes of the patient. The NCT care model addresses the needs of a population of older 
adults congregated in a residential building who want to age in place in the community. This QIP will evaluate the 
feasibility of expanding the NCT model to a non-Toronto Seniors Housing Corporation building at 100 Upper Madison 
Avenue. This building is identified as a Naturally Occurring Retirement Community (NORC). Change ideas are about 
analyzing data we have about people living in the building for two purposes: (1) to apply appropriate interventions that 
meet the health needs of people living in the building; and (2) to observe and understand the logic model for how the 
NCT affects priority indicators for Ontario Health Teams and Ontario Health -- primary care attachment and Ambulatory 
Care Sensitive Conditions -- as well as strategic indicators for Baycrest -- nursing home bed days avoided. 

QIP Target Justification
New patient enrollments to team-based primary care are a priority indicator for Ontario Health as the Primary Care Action Team strives to attach 100% of Ontarians to a family doctor. Attachment for older adults is more challenging than attaching young families. For example, older adults can become intermittently homebound and thus loose attachment to their office-based family doctor. NCT has been successful in attaching older adults with complex health needs to primary care in their building. Only 10% increase in enrollments is proposed as it takes a while to find the older adults in a building who are unattached and orient the team to their needs. As the homebound situation illustrated many residents in NCT buildings already have a family doctor, but office-based care models may no longer meet their needs. Sorting out the optimal attachment requires time and effort.","target_value_text2":"59.40","unit_population_Text2":"% / Population"}

Over the last several years through the implementation of standard bundles of care for central line maintenance, process improvements to achieve reliable bundle adherence, and processes for observing and providing feedback, the rate of CLABSI infections has decreased below the network rate. Following several years of sustained performance below network benchmarks, CLABSI rates increased in 2025, indicating a loss of process reliability rather than a lack of evidence-based prevention strategies. A 10% reduction target (0.948/1000 line days) to move towards the SPS network benchmark is achievable within one year by refocusing on high-leverage process measures, specifically bundle adherence, observation with feedback, and leadership accountability.
